newsitem.title: USA: ALPINE SKIING-WORLD CUP FINALS TO START FAST ON WEDNESDAY. [CORRECTED 16:55 GMT]
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-WORLD CUP FINALS TO START FAST ON WEDNESDAY. [CORRECTED 16:55 GMT]

text.p: (Corrects detail in 10th and 11th paragraphs to make clear Aamodt will compete in the men's downhill)
By Larry Fine
The World Cup Finals start with a bang Wednesday and could end with an historic triumph Sunday following the last of the eight finals to be staged on the slopes of Vail Mountain.

Spring seems to have sprung early here with warm sunshine coaxing resort revellers to doff their jackets. The Finals, aptly, are launched by the most hotly contested individual title race of the Alpine skiing season -- the women's downhill.

After seven women's downhill races, a mere two points separate Russian Warwara Zelenskaja and Heidi Zurbriggen of Switzerland (423-421). Crowding that duo is Renate Goetschl of Austria, 20 points behind the leading Russian, and the fastest down the course in training.

Zelenskaja, hoping to become the first Russian woman ever to claim a World Cup title, zoomed into the lead by sweeping a pair of downhills on the course to be used at next year's Winter Olympics in Japan.
The women's race will be followed by the men's downhill, a discipline that has been utterly dominated by the brilliant Luc Alphand of France.

But Alphand, who easily clinched his third straight title on the strength of four wins this season, has set his sights on an even grander target and is poised to become the first Frenchman since the great Jean-Claude Killy in 1968 to reign as overall champion.
Moreover, Alphand, fourth overall last season, is trying to do it the hard way by focussing solely on the speed events.
He holds a 117-point lead over 1994 overall champion Kjetil Andre Aamodt of Norway, but Alphand will have only one other chance to pad his total when he races in Thursday's Super-G.
Alphand, 31, is in position to claim that crown, too, since he holds a 69-point lead over Austrian Josef Strobl.

The top 25 skiers in each discipline qualify for the finals. Aamodt stands 27th on the downhill list but will still get a chance to win points since skiers with 400 points or more in the overall standings are allowed to enter all events.
The 25-year-old Norwegian all-rounder will also chase points in the Super-G, Saturday's giant slalom and Sunday's slalom.
Half the season titles have already been decided, and Pernilla Wiberg of Sweden has sewn up the women's overall crown.

Wiberg, however, has some work left. The Swede seeks to maintain her lead over Germans Hilde Gerg and Katja Seizinger and add the Super-G title to the slalom championship she ran away with through four wins and two seconds.
Double world champion Deborah Compagnoni of Italy is already assured the giant slalom title.
The men's giant slalom championship belongs to Swiss Michael Von Gruenigen, but the slalom is still a race.

Austrian Thomas Sykora has won five times this season but has yet to shake off compatriot Thomas Stangassinger, who trails by 76 points and needs to win (100 points) or finish second (80 points), while Sykora stumbles.
Besides possibly settling the men's overall title, the slalom will also give adoring fans a taste of the charismatic Alberto Tomba.
Tomba, who hints at ditching his ski racing poles for movie acting roles, has an outside chance of catching France's Sebastien Amiez for the season's bronze.
